name: Fungal acne protocol (Malassezia)

card.summary: Avoiding fatty-acid oils and using antifungals for itchy forehead and body bumps attributed to Malassezia yeast, a recognised condition called Malassezia folliculitis.
card.note: The condition is recognised in dermatology; the specific product-avoidance rules circulating online are not tested in the sources reviewed.

quick.overview:
Fungal acne is the popular name for Malassezia (formerly Pityrosporum) folliculitis, in which yeast that normally lives on skin overgrows in hair follicles and causes itchy, uniform pustules, most often on the upper trunk and sometimes the forehead [1][2]. Online, the term also covers a skincare protocol: avoiding products with certain oils and fatty acids and using antifungal treatments.

Looksmax.org threads show users reporting forehead bumps and flaking that they attribute to fungal acne or seborrheic dermatitis and asking which products to use, with some saying ordinary acne approaches did not help [3][4].
quick.mechanism: Malassezia are lipophilic yeasts that need fatty acids to grow; Wikipedia reports they consume fatty acids with chains of about 11 to 24 carbons [1]. This is the basis for the avoid-certain-oils idea. Research has linked resident Malassezia species to the folliculitis [5].
quick.risks: Malassezia are part of normal skin flora and are linked to several skin conditions including seborrheic dermatitis [6]. Diagnosis is clinical and by distribution [1]; Danish treatment guidelines exist for Malassezia-related disease [7]. Persistent bumps are generally assessed by a dermatologist.

lead: Fungal acne is a popular name for Malassezia folliculitis, also called pityrosporum folliculitis. It is a skin condition in which yeast of the genus Malassezia, a normal part of human skin flora, overgrows within hair follicles and produces itchy papules and pustules [1][6]. Despite the name it is not acne vulgaris, which involves different processes.

Wikipedia describes it as occurring most often on the upper trunk (back, chest, arms) in young to middle-aged adults, with overgrowth associated with oily skin, humidity and conditions such as seborrheic dermatitis or severe dandruff [1]. Malassezia are lipophilic, depending on fatty acids found in skin oils to multiply [1][6].

In looksmaxxing and skincare forums, the phrase also names a protocol: avoiding fatty-acid-containing oils and ingredients in products and using antifungal treatments. Looksmax.org threads show users describing forehead bumps and flaking, sometimes alongside seborrheic dermatitis, and asking what to use [3][4]. The sources reviewed do not trial the protocol as a whole.
infobox: Upper trunk; also forehead and other areas
Itchy, uniform follicular papules and pustules

paras: Malassezia folliculitis arises when Malassezia furfur and related species overgrow and plug hair follicles, producing itchy papules and pustules in a follicular pattern. Diagnosis rests on the pattern and location of lesions [1]. The genus now includes about 14 species of yeast found on all skin surfaces of humans and animals as commensals that can also act as pathogens [8]. Pityriasis versicolor is the only skin disease etiologically tied to Malassezia, while in folliculitis, seborrheic dermatitis and others the yeasts are suggested to contribute [6].

Research comparing seborrheic dermatitis and Malassezia folliculitis has characterised the inflammatory cells in both [9]. A registered clinical study compared Malassezia species proportions in inflammatory and non-inflammatory facial acne lesions in 120 people with acne vulgaris, reflecting ongoing interest in the yeast's role in ordinary acne [10]. A 2009 study concluded that the folliculitis is caused by cutaneous resident Malassezia species [5].

Adherents of the protocol say that because the yeast feeds on certain fatty acids, products containing such oils can worsen bumps and that avoiding them, alongside antifungal products, helps. Forum users describe forehead bumps and flaking that they attribute to fungal acne and report that general skin-care and dietary changes did not resolve them [3][4].

Wikipedia reports Malassezia growth depends on fatty acids of about 11 to 24 carbons [1]. Evidence-based Danish guidelines address treatment of Malassezia-related skin diseases [7]. A 2010 report described photodynamic therapy for recalcitrant Malassezia folliculitis [11]. Reviews note Malassezia infections can be a medical conundrum and can cause more serious disease in immunocompromised patients [12][13]. The sources reviewed do not test an oil-avoidance regimen directly.

Human studies exist on Malassezia folliculitis and related disease, including immunohistochemical work on the skin lesions [9], Danish treatment guidelines [7], and a photodynamic therapy report for resistant cases [11]. No studies found testing the full online fungal acne protocol of avoiding fatty-acid ingredients.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, fungal acne appears in threads where users with stubborn forehead bumps or flaking ask for product recommendations, often alongside seborrheic dermatitis [3][4].

claims.claim: Stubborn forehead bumps that do not respond to normal acne care are fungal acne
claims.believers: One user reports having both seborrheic dermatitis and fungal acne on the forehead, and another says they tried everything including diet and the problem worsened [3][4].
claims.experts: Malassezia folliculitis is a recognised condition with itchy follicular pustules, diagnosed by pattern and location [1]; seborrheic dermatitis is also linked to Malassezia [2][6].

claims.claim: Fatty-acid oils in products feed the yeast and should be avoided
claims.believers: Protocol advocates reason that since the yeast needs fatty acids, avoiding oils containing them reduces flares.
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports Malassezia grows by consuming fatty acids of roughly 11 to 24 carbons [1]; no sources reviewed test product avoidance as a treatment.

claims.believers: Forum users ask for antifungal and related skincare solutions for fungal acne and seborrheic dermatitis [3][4].
claims.experts: Evidence-based Danish guidelines exist for treating Malassezia-related skin diseases [7]; a photodynamic therapy report addressed recalcitrant cases [11].
